html:
Bodéwadmiakiwen is the Potawatomi name for their homeland around the southern end of Lake Michigan, in what are now southern Michigan, northern Indiana, northern Illinois and southeastern Wisconsin. See the main Potawatomi page.

The Potawatomi, or Bodéwadmi, are Anishinaabe people, "keepers of the fire" in the Council of Three Fires with the Ojibwe and the Odawa. They farmed maize and squash, gathered wild rice and hunted, and moved between summer villages and winter hunting camps. They were close partners of the French fur traders of New France.

Through a long series of treaties ending with the Treaty of Chicago in 1833, the United States took their land. Under the Indian Removal Act most were moved west, including on the forced march of 1838 from Indiana known as the Trail of Death. See also Anishinabewaki.
